runs.question: How does the NIST Generative AI Profile describe data privacy risks?

answer.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) treats data privacy as one of its twelve GAI-specific risks, in Section 2.4. Its main concerns are these.

**Training data and consent.** The profile links training on personal data to established privacy principles. The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation. It also notes that developers often keep their sources hidden, so users cannot tell whether their personal information was used. Most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.

**Leakage and memorization.** The profile says models can expose what they learned. During adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. It adds that this may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.

**Inference of personal data.** Risk also arises when a model infers information that was never in its training data. GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources. Even wrong inferences can cause harm: These inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations).

**Downstream harms.** The profile lists exposure harms such as extortion or dignitary harm, and says inferred PII can feed into later decisions. Predictive inferences made by GAI models based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups.

Data privacy also appears as a related concern in other sections. For example, the profile notes that output restrictions can fail against novel prompts and that this is also relevant to CBRN Information or Capabilities, Data Privacy, Information Security, and Obscene, Degrading and/or Abusive Content.

Note: the search tool was unavailable, so I read the Data Privacy section (pages 11–12) directly. I did not check the profile's suggested actions in Section 3 for privacy-specific mitigations, so this answer covers the risk description only.

answer.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) treats data privacy as one of its twelve GAI-specific risks, in Section 2.4. Its main concerns are these.

**Training data and consent.** The profile links training on personal data to established privacy principles. The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation. It also notes that developers often keep their sources hidden, so users cannot tell whether their personal information was used. Most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.

**Leakage and memorization.** The profile says models can expose what they learned. During adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. It adds that this may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.

**Inference of personal data.** Risk also arises when a model infers information that was never in its training data. GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources. Even wrong inferences can cause harm: These inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations).

**Downstream harms.** The profile lists exposure harms such as extortion or dignitary harm, and says inferred PII can feed into later decisions. Predictive inferences made by GAI models based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups.

Data privacy also appears as a related concern in other sections. For example, the profile notes that output restrictions can fail against novel prompts and that this is also relevant to CBRN Information or Capabilities, Data Privacy, Information Security, and Obscene, Degrading and/or Abusive Content.

segments.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) treats data privacy as one of its twelve GAI-specific risks, in Section 2.4. Its main concerns are these.

**Training data and consent.** The profile links training on personal data to established privacy principles.
The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation.
It also notes that developers often keep their sources hidden, so users cannot tell whether their personal information was used.

Most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.
**Leakage and memorization.** The profile says models can expose what they learned.
During adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data.
It adds that this
may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.
**Inference of personal data.** Risk also arises when a model infers information that was never in its training data.
GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources.
Even wrong inferences can cause harm:
These inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations)

.

**Downstream harms.** The profile lists exposure harms such as extortion or dignitary harm, and says inferred PII can feed into later decisions.

.

Data privacy also appears as a related concern in other sections. For example, the profile notes that output restrictions can fail against novel prompts and that this is
